foster

/FOSS-ter/ - rhymes with roster · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Foster means to encourage the growth or development of.

Pairing every rookie with a twenty-year lineman fosters the judgment no manual can teach.

Example

The harbor master lets the middle school log tide readings off the old pier every Friday. It costs him almost nothing — a clipboard, a spare hour, a standing welcome — and it quietly fosters careers: twenty years on, half the pilots licensed on this coast first fell in love with the water holding that clipboard.

Foster is the exact word for what those Fridays do, because foster means to encourage the growth or development of — the harbor master builds the conditions and lets the calling grow on its own. Teach is too narrow: nobody is drilling lessons; the pier, the habit, and the welcome do the growing work.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

nourish: To nourish something is to feed it so it thrives — the picture behind the word is food and steady feeding, even when what is fed is a mind or a hope. Foster builds around rather than feeds: it arranges room, welcome, and conditions, and lets the growth happen on its own.

cultivate: To cultivate is to work at something deliberately so it improves — the farmer cultivates soil and the student cultivates a skill, effort applied directly, day after day. Foster stands a step back: it means inviting growth by arranging conditions and support, then letting the thing develop itself.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

smother: cut off the air a young thing needs

stunt: check growth so it never reaches full size

Where it sits · how lasting and hands-on the support is

encourage → foster → shepherd

encourage vs. foster: Encourage is weaker than foster: a single cheer as the runner passes encourages her for one afternoon, while fostering her talent means supporting its growth month after month.

shepherd vs. foster: Shepherd goes further than foster — fostering arranges room and warmth for growth, while shepherding walks beside the thing through every stage until it arrives.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — foster: food, nourishment (Old English fostor)

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: foster came into English whole, from Old English fostor, 'food, nourishment' — the same age-old family that gave us food and fodder. To foster something is, at the root, to feed it: supply what it needs and let it grow.

Why there's no relative to spot: Fostor never split into prefix and root — English borrowed nothing and bolted nothing on. Its age-old cousins food and fodder share only a prehistoric ancestor, too far back to peel apart today, so the whole word is the root.

Strength Check

Word Choice

warm / constructive

Foster is for growth you arrange rather than force: programs foster curiosity, policies foster trust. Its caring unit-mates divide the labor — nurture is the hands-on feeding and tending of one growing thing, cherish holds something dear without needing it to grow at all. Foster works at arm's length, building conditions.
